title: Bow saws and hand saws: new blades, setting and filing teeth
summary: Keep a bow saw cutting by fitting a fresh blade and restoring the set, and bring an old hand saw back with a file and a saw set. Silky says black tooth tips mean hardened teeth that can't be sharpened with a file: change the blade instead. The danger is the teeth themselves: gloves and a guard on the blade.

steps.text: Look at the tooth tips. Silky says black tips mean induction-hardened teeth, and that hardened blades can't be sharpened with a hand file, so such a blade gets replaced, not filed. Silky says blades whose teeth aren't induction-hardened can be filed (Silky technology, Silky safety). Bahco's bow-saw blades also have induction-hardened points (Bahco 23-24), and TCV calls bow-saw blades not worth resharpening (TCV bowsaws).

To change a bow-saw blade, put gloves on, release the tension lever so the blade goes slack, unhook the blade from its tongue, rivet or nut and bolt, and hook the new one on the same way (Silky safety, TCV bowsaws).
steps.warn: Wear gloves whenever you handle or change a blade (Silky safety).

steps.text: Close the lever to tension the new blade. A frame that can no longer hold a blade tight is finished; sometimes bending its ends apart a little in a vice brings the tension back (TCV bowsaws).
steps.warn: Don't use a saw whose blade is loose, bent or damaged (Silky safety).

steps.text: If a bow-saw blade binds but is still sharp, it has lost its set. Grip it in a vice up to the base of the teeth and bend each tooth back to its own side with pliers, gripping below the hardened tip (TCV bowsaws).
steps.warn: Gripping the hardened tip can snap it off (TCV bowsaws). Wear safety glasses (CCOHS hand saw).

steps.text: For a hand saw that can be filed, clamp it in a vise with the toothline about 2 in (5 cm) above the jaws, and for filing crosscut teeth reclamp it lower, with the bottoms of the gullets about 1/16 in (1.5 mm) above the jaws (Popular Woodworking). Wear safety glasses (CCOHS hand saw).
Joint the teeth: run a flat mill file along the tops, held square to the blade, until every tooth shows a small shiny flat, usually after two to four passes (Popular Woodworking, Workshop Companion).

Set the teeth if the saw binds: with a saw set, bend every other tooth away from you along the whole blade, turn the saw round and do the rest. Use the least set that stops it binding (Popular Woodworking); Workshop Companion bends each tooth about a third of the blade's thickness (Workshop Companion).

Rip saw: hold a taper file level and square across the blade and file each gullet with light, full strokes until the shiny flat on the tooth just disappears, and no further (Popular Woodworking, Workshop Companion).

Crosscut saw: file every other gullet with the file angled back about 15 to 25° from square (Popular Woodworking; Workshop Companion's 75 to 80° to the blade is 10 to 15° from square, so the two overlap only at 15°), taking each flat halfway; then file the gullets you skipped at the opposite angle until every flat is gone (Popular Woodworking).
Lightly stone each side of the teeth with a fine stone, a pass or two and never more than four, to take off the filing burr and even the set (Popular Woodworking).
Test it on scrap like the wood you'll cut. Start slowly so the saw doesn't jump, and press only on the cutting stroke (CCOHS hand saw, Popular Woodworking).
Put the blade guard back on and store bow saws with the tension released (Silky safety, TCV bowsaws, CCOHS hand saw).

notes:
## Which saws can be sharpened
Some saws are sold with induction-hardened teeth: the tips are heated to a very high temperature for a split second, which makes them last about three times longer than untreated teeth. Silky says such teeth can't be sharpened and are recognised by their black tips; it marks the saws whose teeth are not hardened as sharpenable with a file (Silky technology, Silky safety). Bahco's bow-saw blades have high-frequency induction-hardened points (Bahco 23-24). The Conservation Volunteers' tool guide calls bow-saw blades disposable and not worth resharpening (TCV bowsaws). So: a bow saw needs a stock of spare blades, which weigh almost nothing (a 607 mm (24 in) Bahco blade is 60 g) (Bahco 23-24).

Saws with unhardened teeth can be filed (Silky technology): hand saws that aren't induction-hardened, and the big two-person crosscut saws covered below (USFS crosscut saw manual). They are worth looking for in barns, sheds and workshops.

## Bow saws
- **Blades:** Bahco names its blades by the wood they suit; its green-wood blade has raker teeth for easier cutting in green wood, and the sleeve is printed to help pick the right blade (Bahco 23-24). Read the sleeve before you fit one.
- **Fixing:** blades are held by a tongue, a rivet or a nut and bolt. Rivets and nuts get lost; if a tongue breaks, a hole and a small nut and bolt save the saw (TCV bowsaws).
- **Tension:** most frames use a lever, and some have none and are spring-tensioned, so work out how yours slackens before you unhook a blade (TCV bowsaws). Oil the lever pivot now and then. Store the saw with the tension off so the frame keeps its spring (TCV bowsaws).
- **Set:** blades usually lose their set before they go blunt, often from being pinched in a cut, and a blade with no set binds and feels dull. Bending each tooth back to its side with fencing pliers isn't precise, but it works (TCV bowsaws).
- **Guards:** keep a plastic guard on the blade when it isn't cutting; a hand guard on the frame is worth having (TCV bowsaws).

## Hand saws: the four jobs
A hand saw is sharpened in four jobs: set, joint, file, stone (Popular Woodworking lists them in that order and says to check first whether set is needed). The steps above joint first, then set.
- **Set** bends alternate teeth to each side so the cut is wider than the blade. Too little and the saw binds; too much and it cuts loose (stoning takes a little off). Use the least set that stops binding, more for a hand saw than a fine back saw (Popular Woodworking); Workshop Companion bends each tooth about a third of the blade's thickness (Workshop Companion).
- **Jointing** files the tooth tips level so every tooth does the same work (Popular Woodworking, Workshop Companion). If you have to take off more than a third of the tooth height to level them, the teeth need reshaping before filing (Workshop Companion).
- **Filing** brings each tooth back to a point, just until the jointed flat disappears, and no further (Popular Woodworking).
- **Stoning** a light pass on each side takes off burrs and evens the set (Popular Woodworking).

| Saw | Tooth face (rake) | File held | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rip (cuts along the grain) | Near upright, 5–10° back (Popular Woodworking) | Level and square across the blade | Popular Woodworking, Workshop Companion |
| Crosscut (cuts across the grain) | About 15° back | Angled 15–25° from square (Popular Woodworking) or 10–15° from square (Workshop Companion), alternate gullets each way | Popular Woodworking, Workshop Companion |

Workshop Companion holds the file at 75–80° to the blade for crosscut teeth, which is 10–15° from square (Workshop Companion).

### File size by tooth spacing
Saw teeth are counted in points per inch (ppi); teeth per inch (tpi) is one less (Popular Woodworking).

| Points per inch | Taper (triangular) file |
|---|---|
| 12–15 | 4–5 in double extra slim |
| 10–11 | 6 in double extra slim |
| 9 | 6 in extra slim |
| 8 | 6 in slim |
| 5–7 | 7 in slim |
| 3.5–4.5 | 7 in regular |

Source: Popular Woodworking. Joint with a bastard-cut mill file, 10–12 in for hand saws (Popular Woodworking). CCOHS puts general wood cutting at about 4 teeth per inch, coarser for thick stock (CCOHS hand saw).

## Two-person crosscut saws
Big felling and bucking saws from barns are filed in a set order: clean, straighten, joint, fit the rakers, point the cutters, set (USFS crosscut saw manual). The rakers sit a little lower than the cutter points: the Forest Service starts them at about 0.3 mm (0.012 in) below, from 0.2 mm (0.008 in) for hard or dry wood to 0.76 mm (0.030 in) for soft, springy wood. Set starts at about 0.25 mm (0.010 in) for felling saws and 0.4 mm (0.015 in) for heavy bucking saws (USFS crosscut saw manual). The full method, with its special files, raker gauge and spider, is in the manual. Its captions for the slim-taper and mill files say to fit a knuckle guard and a handle (USFS crosscut saw manual).

## Handling blades safely
- Gloves on whenever you handle, change or set a blade (Silky safety).
- Safety glasses while sawing (CCOHS hand saw).
- A guard on the teeth when not cutting; a handle on every file (as on the Forest Service's files); Silky and CCOHS cover the guard on the teeth (Silky safety, CCOHS hand saw, USFS crosscut saw manual).
- Hold the work firmly, start the cut slowly so the blade doesn't jump, and press only on the cutting stroke; too much pressure can break a blade (CCOHS hand saw, hacksaw section).
- Store saws in their sheath, away from damp (Silky safety).

For axes see [Axe and hatchet care](#guides/skill_axe_care); for chainsaws see [Chainsaw chain](#guides/skill_chainsaw_chain).
